screens.title: Particle Filter Localization
screens.subtitle: Monte Carlo Localization for robust, multimodal state estimation

narration.text: In robotics we often need to estimate where a robot is when the uncertainty is complex, multimodal, or non-Gaussian. This lesson introduces particle filters—also called Monte Carlo Localization—which represent beliefs with many sampled hypotheses called particles. You will learn how prediction, sensor update, and resampling work together to concentrate these samples around high probability poses. We will contrast particle filters with Kalman-style filters to show when each approach is appropriate. A practical MATLAB activity will reinforce the ideas: initialize particles uniformly, simulate noisy odometry and range measurements, watch particles converge, then test a kidnapping event and recover with random particle injection. Along the way we’ll highlight two common failure modes: particle degeneracy, where most particles have negligible weight, and impoverishment, where resampling reduces diversity. Understanding these failure modes leads to practical fixes such as adaptive resampling, regularization, and Rao-Blackwellized hybrids. By the end you will know how particle filters work, why they handle multimodal beliefs, and when to prefer them over Kalman filters for real-world localization tasks. Consider: what would you expect to see if a robot starts in a symmetric environment with identical corridors?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Particle filters approximate arbitrary belief distributions with many weighted samples, enabling robust localization under multimodal and non-Gaussian uncertainty.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Particle Filter Localization
Particle Filter Localization
Monte Carlo approach to maintain multiple hypotheses and handle complex, multimodal beliefs.

Why this matters: Kalman-style filters assume a single Gaussian hypothesis. In many startup or symmetric scenes that assumption fails. Particle filters keep many hypotheses and let sensor evidence shape which survive.

What you will do: implement prediction, compute sensor likelihoods, resample systematically, and experiment with adaptive strategies to avoid degeneracy and impoverishment.

Explore Key Topics
Prediction
Propagate particles by motion plus noise so hypotheses move with the robot's odometry.
Update
Weight each particle by how well it predicts the sensor measurement.
Resampling
Draw particles proportional to weight to concentrate samples in probable regions.
Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Probability landscape
Imagine a continuous map of belief: peaks where pose is likely, valleys otherwise. Particles sample that landscape; dense clusters show peaks.
Particles as hypotheses
Each particle holds a pose and weight. Over time prediction moves them, updates scale their weight, and resampling focuses them on peaks.
Quick example
Start with a uniform spread of 1000 particles. After sensing and motion, high-weight particles cluster near the true pose. If the robot is kidnapped, inject random particles and allow sensing to re-establish a cluster.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll practice in this chapter

narration.text: Today’s objectives focus on both conceptual understanding and practical implementation. First, you will learn the Monte Carlo method and how sampling approximates probability distributions. I’ll show why sampling works when distributions are multimodal or non-Gaussian, and give concrete intuition for when a sample set is a good approximation. Second, you will implement a particle filter for localization in a known map. This means writing the prediction step with noisy odometry, computing sensor likelihoods, and performing systematic resampling. Throughout implementation we’ll emphasize readable, testable code so you can visualize particles and evaluate convergence. Third, you’ll learn why resampling is necessary and how particle degeneracy emerges when weights concentrate on a few samples. You’ll test adaptive resampling thresholds and measure the effective number of particles to avoid unnecessary resampling. Fourth, you will compare particle filters with Kalman-style filters and decide which is better for different scenarios such as global localization or well-localized fusion with Gaussian noise. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visualization to help you remember the steps, and a verified competency milestone so you can check your work.

keyIdea.title: Objective set
keyIdea.text: Understand Monte Carlo methods, implement MCL in code, manage resampling challenges, and choose between particle and Kalman filters appropriately.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Details
screens.subtitle: What mastery looks like and quick mnemonics

narration.text: Now let’s make those objectives practical. For Monte Carlo reasoning, picture a landscape where peaks are likely poses and particles are pebbles tossed across it; the pebble density approximates probability mass. For implementation, mastery means you can write a motion update that adds sampled noise, compute ray-casted expected ranges, and multiply likelihoods across beams to form particle weights. For resampling, you should be able to compute the effective number of particles and trigger resampling only when that number falls below a threshold, reducing unnecessary particle impoverishment. For comparison, practice two quick rules of thumb: use Kalman variants when the belief is essentially unimodal and noise is well modeled as Gaussian, and use particle filters for global localization or when sensor noise creates multimodal hypotheses. Each objective has a micro-check: run a simulation, visualize particles as blue dots, true pose as a red dot, and estimated mean as a green dot; if particles converge correctly you pass the milestone. These skills together prepare you to integrate MCL into navigation stacks in simulation or hardware.

screens.title: Why Kalman Filters Fail in Multimodal Cases
screens.subtitle: Understanding the limits of unimodal Gaussian estimators

narration.text: Kalman filters and their extended variants assume the state belief can be summarized as a single Gaussian. That works when uncertainty is roughly unimodal and sensor and motion models are near-linear with Gaussian noise. But in many robot scenarios this assumption does not hold. Imagine a robot placed in a building with two identical corridors. Sensor readings may be consistent with either corridor, producing a bimodal belief. A Kalman filter compresses that into one Gaussian, which typically yields an average position that lies between the corridors — a physically impossible or incorrect estimate. Another case is global localization: when the robot powers on there is effectively a uniform distribution across the map rather than a Gaussian centered somewhere. Kalman filters cannot represent a uniform or multimodal distribution. Particle filters, by contrast, represent belief as many samples and can maintain several distinct hypotheses simultaneously. This distinction matters for design: if your robot may start with large uncertainty or operate in perceptually aliased environments, a particle-based approach preserves multiple hypotheses until sensor evidence rules some out. A common misconception is that more sensors always make Kalman filters sufficient — but if sensors create non-Gaussian likelihoods, sampling is still necessary. Reflect: where in your robot’s environment could ambiguous observations produce multiple equally plausible poses?

keyIdea.title: Limit of Kalman
keyIdea.text: Kalman filters cannot represent multimodal or uniform beliefs; they collapse multiple hypotheses into a single Gaussian average.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Why Kalman Filters Fail
Key claim
Kalman filters assume a single Gaussian; when a belief is multimodal or uniform, that assumption produces misleading averages.
Concrete example
Two identical corridors produce two peaks in belief. A Kalman filter returns their mean, often in a wall or midway location — an incorrect pose estimate.
Misconception
More sensors always fix it. Not necessarily: if sensors produce ambiguous or non-Gaussian likelihoods, the Gaussian assumption still fails.
Key Takeaway

When beliefs are multimodal, prefer a non-parametric representation like particles to avoid averaged, incorrect estimates.

Analogy
Think of the Kalman filter as summarizing a multi-peaked mountain range by a single average height. That loses essential structure. A particle set is like many surveyors sampling the landscape; peaks remain visible as clusters.
Check your understanding
  • Identify one environment in your system that could produce a bimodal belief.
  • Describe why a single Gaussian estimate would be misleading there.

screens.title: Particles: samples as state hypotheses
screens.subtitle: How particles represent complex probability distributions

narration.text: A particle filter represents belief with a collection of particles, where each particle is a hypothesis for the robot’s full state — typically x, y, and heading. Each particle carries a weight proportional to how well that hypothesis explains the sensor data. Collectively, the set of weighted particles approximates the true probability distribution: dense clusters indicate high probability mass, sparse zones indicate low probability. This non-parametric representation has two practical consequences. First, particles can naturally represent multiple separate hypotheses, allowing the filter to hold separate candidate poses until evidence resolves them. Second, the accuracy of the approximation depends on the number and placement of particles: more particles give finer resolution but increase computational cost. A concrete example: when a robot begins with no prior, initialize particles uniformly across free space. After several sense-and-move cycles, particles cluster near the true pose. A common misconception is to treat each particle as an equal vote; in fact, weights matter and resampling redistributes particles according to weight. When teaching or debugging, visualize particle weights with marker size or opacity so you see which hypotheses the filter prefers. Closing question: how many particles would you allocate for a 2D map with many narrow corridors and limited compute budget?

keyIdea.title: Particle nature
keyIdea.text: Particles are weighted hypotheses; their density approximates probability mass and allows multiple distinct modes to coexist.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Particles as Hypotheses
What each particle holds
  • Pose: x, y, theta
  • Weight: likelihood given sensor measurements
  • Optional: history or importance sampling metadata
Concrete example
Initialize 1000 particles uniformly across free space for global localization. After a few steps, high-weight particles cluster near the true pose.
Key Takeaway

Particles give a flexible, sample-based view of belief. Use visualization of weight to understand which hypotheses matter.

Visual debugging
Plot particles as blue dots. Encode weight as size or opacity. Plot true pose as red and estimated mean as green. Watch cluster formation over time to validate behavior.
Misconception
Treating particles as equal votes ignores the crucial role of their weights. Resampling depends on normalized weights, not counts alone.

screens.title: Prediction Step (Motion Update)
screens.subtitle: Propagate particles using motion plus sampled noise

narration.text: The prediction step moves each particle according to the robot’s motion model and injected motion noise. Concretely, if the robot reports a displacement and rotation from odometry, you add that displacement to each particle’s pose and then add sampled noise representing odometry uncertainty. Implementations typically draw Gaussian noise for x, y, and theta and add these to each particle. This step spreads or shifts the particle cloud and encodes our belief about how the robot moved. For example, if the robot moved forward one meter but odometry is noisy, particles will shift forward and smear along the motion direction. A common error is to deterministically add the odometry delta without sampling noise, which underestimates uncertainty and can lead to overconfident particles that later receive low weights. Another subtlety: when using differential-drive robots, apply the correct motion model so heading updates and wheel-slip are modeled properly. After prediction, weights are unchanged; the update phase will reweight particles based on sensor evidence. Practical tip: vectorize or batch your prediction loop to keep simulation fast when using thousands of particles. Question to reflect on: how would the particle cloud behave if your motion noise model is too large or too small relative to actual odometry errors?

keyIdea.title: Motion update
keyIdea.text: Prediction applies odometry with sampled noise to move particles and represent motion uncertainty; do not forget to maintain weight until sensor update.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Prediction Step
Step overview
For each particle, apply the odometry delta and add sampled Gaussian noise to x, y, and theta.
Pseudo-code
for each particle: particle.pose += odometry.delta + sample(noise)
Common mistake
Adding odometry deterministically without noise underestimates uncertainty and causes overconfidence.
Key Takeaway

Model motion uncertainty explicitly by sampling noise during prediction; tune noise to match observed odometry error.

Concrete example
If odometry reports delta_x = 0.5 m and sigma = 0.1 m, sample noise from N(0,0.1) for x, similarly for y and theta, then add to each particle. The cloud shifts forward and expands slightly.
Performance tip
Vectorize sampling and pose updates where possible. Batch ray-casting later in update stage to use GPU or optimized libraries.

screens.title: Update Step (Sensor Likelihood)
screens.subtitle: Weight particles by how well they predict sensor readings

narration.text: The update step assigns a weight to each particle proportional to the likelihood of the observed sensor measurement given that particle’s pose. For range sensors this typically means performing ray-casting from the particle’s pose to compute expected ranges, then computing the likelihood of each observed beam under a Gaussian measurement model. Often we multiply per-beam likelihoods to obtain a particle’s overall weight. In practice it is common to work in log-space or to normalize weights afterward to avoid numerical underflow. For a concrete walkthrough, imagine a particle predicting a wall at 2.1 meters for a beam while the robot measured 2.0 meters; with sigma 0.2 meters the Gaussian likelihood is high and the particle receives a correspondingly large weight. A common misconception is to normalize weights before resampling but forget to handle zero-sum cases; always check for the sum of weights and reinitialize or smooth if all weights are nearly zero. Visualization helps: show large markers for high-weight particles and small faded markers for low-weight ones. Closing reflection: how would sensor noise models change your weight computation for sonar versus lidar?

keyIdea.title: Sensor update
keyIdea.text: Weight particles by likelihood of current measurement; normalize weights and handle numerical issues to prepare for resampling.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Update Step
Key idea
Compute expected sensor reading for each particle, measure likelihood of the actual reading, and set particle weight accordingly.
Per-beam likelihood
weight = product over beams of gaussian_likelihood(observed, expected, sigma)
Numerical note
Multiply many small numbers can underflow. Use log-likelihoods or normalize weights and add a small epsilon before dividing.
Key Takeaway

Design an appropriate sensor noise model and handle normalization robustly so resampling selects meaningful hypotheses.

Concrete example
A particle predicts ranges [2.1, 1.0, 3.0]. Measured ranges are [2.0, 1.2, 2.9] with sigma 0.2. Compute per-beam Gaussian likelihoods and multiply to obtain the particle weight.
Visualization
Render particle size proportional to weight. This makes it obvious which particles the resampler will prefer.

screens.title: Resampling: Systematic Resampling Explained
screens.subtitle: Concentrate particles on high-likelihood regions without bias

narration.text: Resampling draws particles with replacement according to their normalized weights so that high-weight particles are more likely to survive and be duplicated. Systematic resampling is an efficient algorithm that places N equally spaced pointers on the cumulative weight distribution starting from a random offset. For each pointer you select the particle whose cumulative weight exceeds the pointer value. This produces a new particle set where weights are reset to uniform. The provided MATLAB pseudo-code demonstrates this process: normalize weights, compute cumulative sum, choose a random start in the first step interval, then advance by the fixed step to pick all indices. Resampling reduces variance caused by low-weight particles cluttering the set, but it also risks duplicating high-weight particles and losing diversity. Implementing systematic resampling carefully avoids bias and runs in linear time. A practical tip: after resampling, consider adding small Gaussian perturbations (regularization) to maintain diversity. Closing question: how does the choice of random start affect the quality of resampling and variance across runs? Resampling: Systematic Resampling Explained means systematic resampling efficiently redistributes particles by weight, focusing computation on promising hypotheses while remaining unbiased.. In practical terms, concentrate particles on high-likelihood regions without bias. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Resampling purpose
keyIdea.text: Systematic resampling efficiently redistributes particles by weight, focusing computation on promising hypotheses while remaining unbiased.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Resampling
Algorithm sketch
Normalize weights, compute cumulative distribution, choose a random start in [0,1/N), then walk pointers with step 1/N to select particles.
Why systematic
It is low-variance and runs in O(N) time, making it preferred for many MCL implementations.
Key Takeaway

Resampling focuses particles in probable regions but must be balanced with diversity-preserving steps to avoid impoverishment.

Concrete detail
Step size equals 1/num_particles. The start is a uniform random number in [0, step). Using a deterministic start would bias selection across repeated runs.
Misconception
Resampling always improves filter quality. In fact too frequent resampling removes diversity and can hurt recovery from novel states.

screens.title: Systematic Resampling — MATLAB Example
screens.subtitle: Step through a concise resampling implementation

narration.text: Let's walk the MATLAB-style resampling code to see the mechanics in detail. First, normalize weights so they sum to one. Compute the cumulative sum of weights and then create equally spaced selection thresholds starting from a random offset in the first step interval. For each threshold, find the first particle whose cumulative weight exceeds the threshold and copy that particle into the new set, then reset its weight to uniform. This produces new_particles where all weights are equal. Watch for numerical issues: if the sum of weights is zero due to underflow, you must reinitialize weights uniformly or add a small constant. A common debugging technique is to plot cumulative weights and overlay the equally spaced thresholds to visually confirm selection. The code block below mirrors the textbook pseudo-code and includes comments on the normalization and random start. After you implement it, run unit tests where a single particle has high weight and confirm it is duplicated approximately proportional to its weight. How would you modify this routine to return indices only and avoid copying large state structures in memory-constrained systems?

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Systematic resampling uses cumulative weights and uniformly spaced pointers; validate with visualization and guard against zero-sum weights.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Resampling Code
Annotated MATLAB snippet
% Normalize weights
weights = [particles.weight];
weights = weights / sum(weights);

% Cumulative sum
cumulative = cumsum(weights);

% Systematic resampling
new_particles = particles; % preallocate
step = 1 / num_particles;
start = rand() * step;

for i = 1:num_particles
    threshold = start + (i-1)*step;
    idx = find(cumulative >= threshold, 1);
    new_particles(i) = particles(idx);
    new_particles(i).weight = 1 / num_particles;
end
This code shows the essential operations. Replace copies with index-based selection to reduce memory overhead if particle objects are large.
Practical checks
  • Plot cumulative and thresholds to verify selection visually.
  • Ensure weights sum is non-zero; add small epsilon if needed.
  • Test edge cases: single dominant particle, uniform weights, and numerical rounding.
Key Takeaway

Understand pointers on the cumulative distribution and guard against numerical edge cases when implementing resampling.

screens.title: Particle Degeneracy and Impoverishment
screens.subtitle: Why particles collapse and how that harms tracking

narration.text: Particle degeneracy occurs when after many update steps most particles carry negligible weight and only a few particles dominate the weight distribution. This means the effective sample size is small and the filter’s approximation is poor. Resampling reduces degeneracy by eliminating low-weight particles and duplicating high-weight ones, but resampling too often causes particle impoverishment: duplicated particles decrease diversity, making the filter brittle to unexpected motions or a kidnapping event. A concrete example: after a long sequence with stable sensors, a handful of particles may hold 90 percent of the total weight; repeated resampling will replicate those few and remove others, preventing exploration of alternate hypotheses. To diagnose degeneracy compute the effective number of particles, N_eff = 1 / sum(w_i^2); when N_eff falls below a threshold, resample. A misconception is that simply increasing particle count always fixes degeneracy — while more particles help, without proper resampling policy and diversity maintenance they still degrade. The practical takeaway: measure N_eff, resample adaptively, and apply diversity-preserving steps like jittering or injecting a fraction of random particles. How would you select the N_eff threshold for your robot and compute budget?

keyIdea.title: Degeneracy issue
keyIdea.text: Degeneracy reduces effective samples; adaptive resampling and diversity injections help preserve tracking ability and recovery potential.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Degeneracy & Impoverishment
Definitions
Degeneracy: most weights near zero. Impoverishment: loss of diversity after resampling duplicates high-weight particles.
Measure
Effective particles N_eff = 1 / sum(w_i^2). Trigger resampling when N_eff < threshold.
Key Takeaway

Monitor effective sample size and balance resampling frequency with diversity-preserving steps to avoid long-term failure.

Concrete scenario
If one particle holds most probability, resampling will duplicate it. If the robot then moves unexpectedly, the filter may lose the true pose because there are too few distinct hypotheses.
Check
Compute N_eff over time and plot it. Resample only when the curve dips below your chosen threshold to avoid unnecessary impoverishment.

screens.title: Adaptive Resampling & Effective Particle Count
screens.subtitle: When to resample and how to measure weight concentration

narration.text: Adaptive resampling uses a quantitative trigger instead of resampling at every step. The common metric is the effective number of particles, N_eff = 1 / sum(w_i^2). When N_eff is high, weights are well distributed and resampling is unnecessary; when N_eff falls below a chosen threshold, resampling reduces degeneracy. Selecting the threshold trades off computation and diversity: a high threshold triggers resampling often and risks impoverishment, a low threshold delays resampling and allows degeneracy to persist. To choose a threshold, profile your system: test different values and observe recovery time after perturbations like kidnapping. Implementations often set threshold to a fraction of total particles, such as N/2. When computing N_eff, remember to normalize weights first and handle numerical stability by adding epsilon if weights are extremely small. A practical workflow: compute N_eff each cycle, only resample when below threshold, and optionally inject a small fraction of random particles at resample time to maintain exploration. Final thought: adaptive resampling keeps computation efficient and helps balance the twin risks of degeneracy and impoverishment. Adaptive Resampling & Effective Particle Count means use n_eff to decide when to resample; tune threshold to balance degeneracy reduction and diversity preservation.. In practical terms, when to resample and how to measure weight concentration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Adaptive policy
keyIdea.text: Use N_eff to decide when to resample; tune threshold to balance degeneracy reduction and diversity preservation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Adaptive Resampling
Effective particles
Compute N_eff = 1 / sum(w_i^2) after normalizing weights. Use this scalar to assess weight concentration.
Policy
If N_eff < threshold (e.g., N/2), perform resampling; otherwise skip to save computation and preserve diversity.
Key Takeaway

Adaptive resampling reduces unnecessary resampling and helps keep particle diversity when the weight distribution is broad.

Practical adjustments
  • Add epsilon when normalizing to prevent division by zero.
  • Optionally inject a small fraction of random particles on resample to aid recovery.
  • Tune threshold empirically for your sensor and motion noise characteristics.

screens.title: Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filters
screens.subtitle: Hybrid approach: particles for nonlinear parts, Kalman filters for linear subspaces

narration.text: Rao-Blackwellized particle filters decompose the state into parts that can be handled analytically and parts that need sampling. Typically, linear Gaussian substructures are estimated with Kalman filters conditioned on sampled variables. This reduces the dimensionality of the particle space and improves efficiency: particles represent only the nonlinear or discrete components while the Kalman updates handle continuous linear sub-states. A concrete robotics example is simultaneous localization and mapping where the robot pose is sampled by particles while landmark positions are tracked by Kalman filters conditioned on each particle. The main benefit is lower variance and fewer particles required for comparable accuracy. A misconception is that Rao-Blackwellization always reduces implementation complexity; in fact it often adds architectural complexity because you maintain a bank of local filters per particle and must manage their state and covariance. Consider computation-memory trade-offs: Rao-Blackwellization saves particle count but increases per-particle Kalman work. Closing question: which parts of your robot state could be modeled analytically and which require sampling? Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filters means rao-blackwellization reduces particle dimensionality by using analytic filters for linear parts and particles for the nonlinear parts, improving efficiency at some engineering cost.. In practical terms, hybrid approach: particles for nonlinear parts, kalman filters for linear subspaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hybrid strategy
keyIdea.text: Rao-Blackwellization reduces particle dimensionality by using analytic filters for linear parts and particles for the nonlinear parts, improving efficiency at some engineering cost.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Rao-Blackwellized PF
Concept
Decompose state and apply analytic Kalman updates to linear-Gaussian parts conditioned on sampled variables. Particles represent only the remaining uncertainty.
Robotics example
Pose sampled by particles, landmark positions estimated with Kalman filters conditioned on each sampled pose.
Key Takeaway

Use Rao-Blackwellization when parts of the state are linear and Gaussian to reduce particle dimensionality and improve efficiency.

Trade-offs
  • Fewer particles required for similar accuracy.
  • Increased implementation complexity and per-particle compute for Kalman updates.
  • Requires careful bookkeeping of filter states per particle.

screens.title: Regularization and Random Particle Injection
screens.subtitle: Keeping diversity and recovering from kidnapping

narration.text: Regularization and random particle injection are practical tools to maintain diversity and enable recovery when the robot is unexpectedly moved. Regularization applies a small random perturbation to particles after resampling so duplicated particles spread slightly, preserving local diversity. Random particle injection places a small fraction of particles uniformly across the map at resample time so that entirely new hypotheses remain available. This is particularly valuable for kidnapping scenarios: if the true pose suddenly moves far from the dominant cluster, injected particles may land near the true pose and, if sensor evidence supports them, grow into a new cluster. For example, inject 1–5 percent of particles uniformly during resampling; tune the fraction based on how frequently kidnapping is expected and your particle budget. A misconception is to inject too many particles, effectively discarding signal—treat injection as exploratory noise, not a reset. Practice by simulating a kidnapping at step 50 and observe whether injections allow the filter to recover within reasonable time. Final reflection: what injection fraction balances recovery speed with steady-state localization quality for your system? Regularization and Random Particle Injection means use small perturbations and occasional random particle injection to preserve diversity and enable recovery from large unexpected state changes.. In practical terms, keeping diversity and recovering from kidnapping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Diversity tools
keyIdea.text: Use small perturbations and occasional random particle injection to preserve diversity and enable recovery from large unexpected state changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › Regularization & Injection
Regularization
After resampling, add small Gaussian noise to particle poses to avoid identical duplicates and maintain local exploration.
Random injection
Insert a small percentage of particles sampled uniformly across free space at resample time to allow recovery from large errors.
Key Takeaway

Use both small jitter and occasional random injection to preserve the filter’s ability to explore and recover.

Practical example
In a 1000-particle filter, injecting 10–50 random particles (1–5%) at resample time helps recover from kidnapping without disrupting steady-state performance.
Misconception
Random injection is not a full reset. Treat it as an exploratory safeguard and tune the rate conservatively.

screens.title: Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) and Hands-On Activity
screens.subtitle: Putting prediction, update, and resample together in simulation

narration.text: Monte Carlo Localization applies the particle filter cycle in a known map for mobile robot localization. Start by distributing particles uniformly across free space for global localization. Each timestep perform prediction using noisy odometry, compute sensor likelihoods (often via ray-casting), normalize weights, compute N_eff to decide on resampling, then resample systematically and optionally apply regularization and random injection. The hands-on MATLAB activity suggested in the chapter walks you through creating a 20 by 20 grid map, defining rectangular obstacles, and simulating a circular true trajectory. Use sigma 0.1 meters for odometry noise and sigma 0.2 meters for range sensors as a baseline. Initialize 1000 particles and visualize blue particles, the red true position, and a green estimated mean. Run for 100 steps and at step 50 simulate a kidnapping by teleporting the true pose to a random location; observe whether injected particles let the filter recover. This activity demonstrates the dynamics of convergence, the effects of degeneracy, and the value of injection and adaptive policies. After running experiments, reflect on tuning: particle count, noise parameters, N_eff threshold, and injection fraction. Which tuning had the biggest effect on recovery speed and steady-state accuracy?

keyIdea.title: MCL workflow
keyIdea.text: Iterate prediction, update, and adaptive resampling in simulation; visualize particles and experiment with kidnapping and injection to validate behavior.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.3 › MCL & Hands-On
Activity summary
Create a 20×20 grid map, simulate a circular true trajectory, add Gaussian odometry and range noise, initialize 1000 particles, and run 100 steps with visualization.
Simulation parameters
Odometry sigma = 0.1 m, range sigma = 0.2 m, particles = 1000, steps = 100, kidnapping at step 50.
Key Takeaway

Hands-on simulation makes resampling effects, degeneracy, and recovery immediately visible—use it to tune parameters and policies.

Guided checklist
  1. Generate free-space particle set uniformly.
  2. Implement motion_update with sampled noise.
  3. Implement sensor_update with ray-casting and likelihoods.
  4. Compute N_eff and apply adaptive resampling.
  5. Inject random particles and regularize after resample if needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to carry forward

narration.text: Summarize and lock in three essential ideas. First, particle filters are non-parametric: they approximate arbitrary distributions by sampling many weighted hypotheses, allowing representation of multimodal and non-Gaussian beliefs. Second, the predict-update-resample cycle drives localization: prediction spreads particles by motion plus noise, update assigns weights via sensor likelihoods, and resampling concentrates computation on promising hypotheses. Third, managing degeneracy and impoverishment is central: measure the effective particle count, resample adaptively, and use regularization or random injection to maintain the ability to recover from unexpected motions or kidnapping. Keep these points in mind when choosing an estimator: use Kalman-style filters for unimodal Gaussian problems and particle filters when global uncertainty or perceptual aliasing creates multiple plausible states. As you apply these concepts, balance particle count, noise models, and resampling policies to meet accuracy and compute constraints.

Particle filter
Non-parametric sample-based belief representation that supports multimodal distributions.
Predict → Update → Resample
The core MCL cycle: motion update, sensor likelihood weighting, and resampling to focus particles.
Degeneracy & recovery
Monitor effective sample size, use adaptive resampling, regularization, and random injection to preserve diversity and enable recovery.
Summary takeaway
Use particle filters when you need to represent multiple hypotheses or non-Gaussian noise. Balance particle count and resampling strategy to meet accuracy and compute constraints.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical Notes
screens.subtitle: Three implementation tips to apply immediately

narration.text: Finish with three practical notes you can apply right away. First, always visualize particles, true pose, and estimated mean during development; visualization is the fastest way to find bugs in motion, update, or resampling code. Second, prefer adaptive resampling driven by the effective particle count rather than resampling every loop—this reduces unnecessary impoverishment and saves C P U. Third, test kidnapping scenarios and include small random particle injections or Rao-Blackwellized structure when recovery or efficiency is essential. These pragmatic checks and tests will determine whether your MCL runs reliably in simulation and on real robots. Try varying particle count and noise parameters to see how convergence and recovery change, and document a configuration that balances accuracy with your computational budget.
